mcqs.question: A team plans to freeze feature work and rewrite their monolith from scratch, cutting over on one release day. What is the main risk this approach carries?
options: The rewrite becomes a multi-year moving target while the business either stalls on features or keeps changing the old system in parallel
Rewrites always produce lower-quality code than the original system
A single cutover day is technically impossible to schedule
Big-bang rewrites are only risky for very small systems, not large ones
mcqs.explanation: The real risk is time and drift: rewriting from scratch tends to take far longer than planned, and during that time the business either freezes features (losing ground) or keeps changing the old system (making the rewrite chase a moving target). Rewrites aren't inherently lower quality, a cutover day is schedulable in principle, and the risk actually grows with system size and complexity, not shrinks.

mcqs.question: During a dual-write window while extracting an Inventory service, what is the main risk to manage?
options: Dual-writing eliminates the need for any data validation before cutover
The two writes (to the old and new stores) can never be perfectly atomic, so drift between them must be actively monitored
The old monolith database can simply be deleted as soon as dual-writing starts
Dual-write windows are risk-free and can be left running indefinitely as a permanent architecture
mcqs.explanation: Writing to two separate stores for the same operation can't be made perfectly atomic, so the two copies can drift apart — that's exactly why the window should be short and actively monitored. Dual-writing doesn't remove the need to validate data, deleting the old database before cutover would destroy your fallback, and treating it as permanent ignores its inherent fragility.

mcqs.question: A production system with active users and ongoing feature requests needs to move off a monolith. Per the compare table, which approach better fits this situation, and why?
options: Big-bang rewrite, since it produces a cleaner final architecture regardless of the migration path
Strangler fig migration, since each slice ships and validates independently while feature work continues on unmigrated parts
Big-bang rewrite, since it is always faster in total calendar time
Neither is appropriate for a system with active users
mcqs.explanation: For a live system with ongoing feature demands, the strangler pattern lets each migrated slice ship and be validated on its own while the rest of the system keeps evolving normally — exactly the scenario where a frozen, all-or-nothing rewrite is riskiest. The end architecture's cleanliness doesn't depend on the migration path chosen, big-bang rewrites are typically not faster in total time, and migration is very much appropriate for live systems — it's the default recommended case.

mcqs.question: A team migrated their highest-value features off the monolith years ago and left the strangler proxy routing a small amount of low-traffic legacy functionality indefinitely. What is the likely long-term cost?
options: There is no cost, since low-traffic code by definition doesn't matter
The proxy automatically finishes the migration on its own after enough time passes
Leaving the proxy in place has no effect on on-call complexity
Engineers permanently pay the cost of understanding two architectures, and the leftover legacy piece often turns out to gate something nobody wants to touch
mcqs.explanation: A half-migrated system means the team indefinitely carries the cognitive and on-call cost of two architectures, and the 'low-traffic' remainder often turns out to gate something important (a compliance report, an admin tool) that keeps getting deprioritized. Low traffic doesn't mean zero importance, a proxy doesn't migrate anything on its own, and running two architectures does add real on-call complexity.
